props.title: The Devil's Backbone
props.initialSlug: Orphaned boy uncovers ghost's dark wartime secret

sections.content: The Devil's Backbone (2001) stands as Guillermo del Toro's haunting masterpiece of Gothic horror, setting a ghost story against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War. The film established del Toro's signature blend of political allegory and supernatural elements that would later flourish in Pan's Labyrinth (2006). Set in a remote orphanage, the film follows Carlos, a young boy who encounters the spirit of Santi, a murdered orphan whose death holds dark secrets. Del Toro crafts a ghost story that's more melancholic than terrifying, using supernatural elements to explore very real human brutality.

sections.content: The film's visual language draws from Spanish Gothic traditions while subverting classic ghost story tropes. Unlike the jump-scares of mainstream horror, del Toro uses Santi's ghost - perpetually leaking blood that floats upward like seaweed - as a mournful presence demanding justice. This approach influenced later sophisticated horror films like The Others (2001) and The Orphanage (2007), which similarly use ghosts as tragic figures rather than mere agents of terror.

Del Toro's masterful use of the orphanage setting creates a microcosm of Spanish society during the Civil War. The film shares thematic DNA with Spirit of the Beehive (1973) and Cría Cuervos (1976), Spanish classics that also use children's perspectives to examine political trauma. The unexploded bomb in the courtyard serves as both literal threat and potent metaphor for the war's looming violence. SUBHEAD: Gothic Horror as Political Allegory

movies.title: Cría Cuervos
movies.slug: A haunting Spanish drama about a young girl coping with loss in Franco's Spain, blending reality and imagination.

sections.content: The film exemplifies how horror can address historical trauma, similar to how The Innocents (1961) used ghost stories to explore psychological repression. Del Toro's approach influenced later films like Under the Shadow (2016) and A Tale of Two Sisters (2003), which blend cultural specificity with supernatural elements to process national trauma.
